# Duplicated Sim Code Instead of a Shared Package

**Decision:** keep the shared simulation logic as **two hand-synchronised copies** — one in
`client/src`, one in `server/src` — rather than extracting it into a workspace package both import.

> "`server/src/sim/movement.ts` — server-authoritative `stepPlayer` — **intentionally duplicated**
> from `client/src/game/player/playerController.ts`, not imported, so the server has no runtime
> dependency on client code."
> — browser_game_stickfps/docs/specs/task-4.1.md, 2026-07-25

Three pairs are duplicated this way: the movement step, the weapon rules/definitions, and the message
type definitions.

## The reason, stated and narrow

**The server must have no runtime dependency on client code.** Under
[[server-authoritative-netcode]] the server is the security boundary; a shared package makes it
import from the same tree as the untrusted half, and every change to client rendering code becomes a
change that can reach the authority. Duplication makes the boundary structural instead of a
convention.

The secondary effect is deployment shape: the two halves build and ship independently
([[split-frontend-backend-hosting]]), with no workspace root to resolve, which keeps the
[[docker]] image and the Render build simple.

## The cost, which is real

Duplicated movement code that drifts breaks
[[client-side-prediction-and-reconciliation]] silently — prediction error grows and the blend never
catches up, and it manifests as "the controls feel bad", not as a failing test. Duplicated message
types break the wire format at runtime rather than at compile time.

What makes it survivable here is that the client copies are **explicitly cosmetic**: the client
predicts with them, and nothing they compute is ever scored. A divergence produces visual drift, not
a wrong kill. That asymmetry is the precondition for this trade, and it is the thing to check before
copying the pattern — duplication is affordable exactly where one copy is not authoritative.

Extraction into a shared workspace package is recorded in the spec as a **named follow-up**, not as
an oversight.

## Alternative rejected

A `packages/shared` workspace importing into both — the conventional answer. Rejected on the runtime
dependency argument above. Note it would not have removed the need for [[fixed-timestep-simulation]]
to run at an identical rate on both sides; a shared package makes the *code* identical, not the
*schedule*.
